official_name: Neurocognitive Disorder Due to Traumatic Brain Injury
plain_title: Thinking changes after a head injury
one_liner: Lasting trouble with memory, attention, or thinking after a blow to the head, long after the early recovery.
in_simple_words: A brain injury from a fall, crash, assault, sport, or blast can leave lasting changes in thinking. People may think more slowly, lose focus, forget things, and struggle to plan. Mood, temper, energy, and sleep often change too. The diagnosis applies when these last beyond the early weeks. Most mild injuries (concussions) heal within weeks. Severe or repeated injuries can cause lasting problems. Rehab helps. So does knowing that the person has a real injury.
what_it_can_feel_like: Six months after the crash I looked fine. I couldn't follow a recipe or a conversation in a noisy room.
The anger scared me more than the memory problems. Nobody had warned me that was part of it.
Brain injury rehab was slow and boring and it gave me my job back.
common_signs: A head injury with blackout, confusion, memory loss, or nerve signs
Lasting trouble with attention, memory, thinking speed, or planning
Fatigue, headaches, sleep problems, sensitivity to noise or light
Short temper, mood swings, depression, anxiety, or personality change
Difficulties at work, school, or in relationships
Problems that go on longer than expected for that injury

myths_vs_facts.myth: If the scan is clear, the brain is fine.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Scans miss much of the damage in brain injury. Symptoms and assessment of thinking matter more than imaging.
Most concussions recover, but some don't, and repeated concussions add up. Rest, graded return, and follow-up matter.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Personality change after brain injury is the person's choice.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Injury to the frontal lobes directly affects impulse control, mood, and judgment. Understanding this helps families cope.

how_common.plain: Traumatic brain injuries are very common, with millions of emergency visits a year in the US alone. Most are mild and recover; a minority leave lasting cognitive problems.
how_common.figure: Over 2 million TBI-related emergency visits a year in the US (CDC); most are mild; persistent NCD follows a minority, more after moderate–severe or repeated injury
how_common.note: CDC figure from memory; needs confirmation.

what_helps.plain_summary: Treatment is rehab. Thinking rehab retrains attention and memory and teaches ways around the gaps. Occupational therapy helps with daily tasks and work. Physio helps the body. Talk therapy helps with mood, anger, and adjusting. Medication, prescribed and monitored by a doctor, may be used for depression, sleep, or headaches. Teaching the person and family what to expect is a core part. A step-by-step return to work or study, with adjustments, improves results. Avoiding another injury matters, especially in sport.
evidence_based_options: Psychological therapy for mood, anger, and adjustment
Graded return to work or study; medication for specific symptoms, prescribed and monitored by a doctor
self_help_that_supports_care: Pacing: rest before fatigue, not after
External memory aids: notes, alarms, one notebook
Quiet environments and one task at a time
Brain injury peer groups, which understand invisible injury

when_to_reach_out: If thinking, mood, or energy haven't come back to normal weeks after a head injury, ask a doctor about a brain injury check and rehab. Go to emergency care for a worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, a seizure, or sleepiness after any head injury.
is_not: Normal recovery from a concussion over a few weeks isn't this disorder. PTSD after the same accident can look similar and is treated differently; both can happen. Dementia from other causes isn't counted unless the injury set it off.
hope_note: The brain keeps healing for a long time after injury, and rehabilitation keeps building on it. Many people return to full lives, often with new strategies.

content_notes: Site-wide crisis link stays one tap away.

in_young_people: Children's brains are still growing, so the effects of an injury can show up over time, especially in learning and behaviour. Sport concussion rules and school support plans matter.
